L0@P0: NeuMMU: Architectural Support for Efficient
L1@P0: Address Translations in Neural Processing Units
L2@P0: Bongjoon Hyun Youngeun Kwon Yujeong Choi John Kim Minsoo Rhu
L3@P0: School of Electrical Engineering
L4@P0: KAIST
L5@P0: {bongjoon.hyun, yekwon, yjchoi0606, jjk12, mrhu}@kaist.ac.kr
L6@P0: Abstract—To satisfy the compute and memory demands of
L7@P0: deep neural networks, neural processing units (NPUs) are widely
L8@P0: being utilized for accelerating deep learning algorithms. Similar
L9@P0: to how GPUs have evolved from a slave device into a mainstream
L10@P0: processor architecture, it is likely that NPUs will become firstclass citizens in this fast-evolving heterogeneous architecture
L11@P0: space. This paper makes a case for enabling address translation
L12@P0: in NPUs to decouple the virtual and physical memory address
L13@P0: space. Through a careful data-driven application characterization study, we root-cause several limitations of prior GPU-centric
L14@P0: address translation schemes and propose a memory management
L15@P0: unit (MMU) that is tailored for NPUs. Compared to an oracular
L16@P0: MMU design point, our proposal incurs only an average 0.06%
L17@P0: performance overhead.
L18@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L19@P0: The complexity of deep neural network (DNN) based deep
L20@P0: learning (DL) algorithms are scaling up rapidly. To meet the
L21@P0: demands of these computation-hungry algorithms, acceleratorcentric systems based on GPUs or custom-designed ASICs for
L22@P0: DNNs, often referred to as neural processing units (NPUs),
L23@P0: are widely being utilized for accelerating DL. Similar to how
L24@P0: GPUs have evolved into a mainstream processor architecture,
L25@P0: it is expected that NPUs will become first-class citizens in
L26@P0: heterogeneous computing platforms due to the increasing
L27@P0: number of application domains it is expected to accelerate.
L28@P0: Based on these trends, an important challenge that arises is
L29@P0: how NPUs should be exposed to the end-user and how the
L30@P0: memory address space be exposed to the NPUs. Traditionally,
L31@P0: the I/O attached accelerators such as GPUs had separate
L32@P0: memory address space than the CPU, forcing programmers
L33@P0: to manage these distinct address regions through manual
L34@P0: memory allocations, data copies, etc. As GPUs evolved into
L35@P0: having a proper memory management unit (MMU) [1], [2],
L36@P0: [3], programmers are now given the illusion of a unified CPUGPU memory address [4], [5] allowing CPU and GPU to
L37@P0: share a globally addressable memory regardless of whether
L38@P0: the physical memory is shared or separate. Other key features
L39@P0: enabled by GPU MMUs include memory oversubscription [6],
L40@P0: [7], NUMA [8], [9], [10], and spatial sharing of a single GPU
L41@P0: substrate while supporting page-granularity protections [11].
L42@P0: Unfortunately, these features are yet to be available for NPUs
L43@P0: because they currently do not have an MMU for decoupling
L44@P0: virtual addresses against physical addresses. Consequently,
L45@P0: the range of applications that can utilize these accelerators
L46@P0: is limited. For instance, NPUs cannot page-fault on missing

L72@P0: set of a target DNN application must precisely fit within the
L73@P0: physical memory capacity: otherwise, the runtime crashes [12].
L74@P0: Given this landscape, we argue that future NPUs will
L75@P0: need dedicated architectural support for virtual-to-physical
L76@P0: address translation services. Conventional wisdom in DNN’s
L77@P0: memory access characteristics is that they are highly regular
L78@P0: and predictable, allowing the compiler to optimally decide how
L79@P0: much memory to allocate and when/where to read/write data
L80@P0: for NPU processing, obviating the need for fine-grained, pagelevel translations or NUMA capabilities. While such property
L81@P0: held true for regular, “dense” DNNs (e.g, convolutional,
L82@P0: recurrent, and multi-layer perceptrons, CNNs/RNNs/MLPs),
L83@P0: emerging DL workloads employing embedding layers exhibit a
L84@P0: highly “sparse”, irregular, and random memory access pattern
L85@P0: over a large embedding lookup table (Figure 1). Recent studies
L86@P0: from Baidu and Facebook [19], [20] state that their productionlevel DL workloads using embeddings already reached close
L87@P0: to 100 GBs of memory footprint because of these embedding
L88@P0: tables, even for inference (Section III-A). Because current
L89@P0: NPUs incorporate only tens of GBs of local memory, these
L90@P0: memory-limited DL applications must partition its memory
L91@P0: usage across CPU−NPU (or NPUm−NPUn under multiNPU systems [21], [22]), incurring frequent CPU↔NPU (or
L92@P0-1: arXiv:1911.06859v1 [cs.AR] 15 Nov 2019NPU↔NPU) data transfers. Because of the irregular, random
L93@P1: memory access nature of embedding layers, an MMU-less
L94@P1: NPU must rely on the CPU to manually orchestrate data
L95@P1: transfers on its behalf, experiencing significant performance
L96@P1: overheads (Section V). Similar to how demand paging or
L97@P1: NUMA has been a crucial component in CPUs (and now GPUs,
L98@P1: especially under CPU-GPU [8] or multi-GPU [9] systems),
L99@P1: we believe that a robust NPU address translation service will
L100@P1: enable a more diverse range of emerging, memory-hungry
L101@P1: DL applications to be seamlessly executed on NPUs without
L102@P1: falling into the pitfalls and performance overheads of manual
L103@P1: management of NPU physical memory.
L104@P1: To this end, this paper explores the design space of NPU
L105@P1: MMUs and identifies and addresses the unique challenges in
L106@P1: adding architectural support for address translation based on
L107@P1: a data-driven approach. Our study consists of two main parts:
L108@P1: 1) Design space exploration of an NPU MMU that enables
L109@P1: robust address translation for conventional dense DNN
L110@P1: layers (Section IV)
L111@P1: 2) Highlighting the usefulness of an NPU MMU in efficiently handling sparse embedding layers via finegrained NUMA access or page-migration (Section V)
L112@P1: As such, we start by first employing prior GPU-centric
L113@P1: MMU solutions [1], [3] that utilize I/O memory management
L114@P1: units (IOMMUs) to handle NPU address translations for
L115@P1: conventional, dense DNNs. Interestingly, our analysis shows
L116@P1: that, due to the fundamental architectural differences between
L117@P1: GPUs and NPUs, a naive IOMMU address translation incurs
L118@P1: significant performance overhead even for these dense DNNs.
L119@P1: Concretely, while GPUs commonly use the on-chip SRAM for
L120@P1: register-files and caches, NPUs almost exclusively utilize its
L121@P1: SRAM for software managed scratchpads. The activations and
L122@P1: weights the NPUs operate on are typically multi-dimensional
L123@P1: tensors, mapped to a traditional, linear (1D) memory subsystem. These tensors are much larger than the scratchpad,
L124@P1: so the DMA unit blocks the activations/weights into tiles
L125@P1: and sequence them across multiple (tile) fetch operations via
L126@P1: double-buffering. As these tiles are also multi-dimensional
L127@P1: tensors, fetching them into the scratchpad involves projecting
L128@P1: the multi-dimensional coordinates into the linear space of
L129@P1: DRAM memory. A single tile is therefore decomposed into
L130@P1: minimum number of linearized memory transactions, which
L131@P1: can be up to several thousands, because a tile is sized at several
L132@P1: MBs to maximally utilize the scratchpad. Consequently, a
L133@P1: single tile fetch invokes significant bursts of page translations
L134@P1: that conventional MMUs fail to effectively capture, leading
L135@P1: to an average 95% performance overhead.
L136@P1: Overall, we observe that the bursty nature of scratchpadbased NPU address translation traffic renders the translation
L137@P1: throughput of baseline IOMMU’s (multiple) page-table walkers
L138@P1: (PTWs) a key performance bottleneck. As a result, unlike
L139@P1: GPUs which are optimized for translation locality [1], [3],
L140@P1: we argue that NPU MMUs should be designed for high
L141@P1: translation throughput first and locality second. To this respect,
L142@P1: we propose a throughput-centric NPU MMU (NeuMMU) design
L143@P1: that effectively handles high burst of translation requests.
L144@P1: NeuMMU is designed to reduce the address translation overhead
L145@P1: by leveraging the deterministic memory access behavior of
L146@P1: dense DNNs and the inherent translation locality therein.
L147@P1: Concretely, while TLBs are not as effective for NPUs than
L148@P1: CPUs or GPUs, we identify how translation burst locality
L149@P1: exists within a given tile fetch in DNNs. To capture such
L150@P1: intra-tile translation locality, we first propose our novel
L151@P1: pending request merging buffer (PRMB) microarchitecture
L152@P1: as a translation bandwidth filtering mechanism to reduce
L153@P1: the number of distinct page-table walks concurrently inflight, boosting effective translation bandwidth. In addition
L154@P1: to the PRMB microarchitecture, the MMU also requires high
L155@P1: concurrent address translations and we evaluate the need for
L156@P1: a larger number of PTWs to maximize translation throughput.
L157@P1: Unfortunately, the large amount of translations can incur
L158@P1: significant power overheads due to the additional memory
L159@P1: accesses involved in the translation process. We make the key
L160@P1: observation that dense DNN layers exhibit a regular dataflow,
L161@P1: rendering its memory access patterns to be highly deterministic
L162@P1: with only a handful of key data structures being manipulated
L163@P1: (i.e., input/output activations, weights). This allows us to
L164@P1: employ a lightweight translation path “register”, unlike the
L165@P1: traditional MMU cache [23], that effectively filters down on the
L166@P1: number of translation-invoked DRAM accesses (a reduction
L167@P1: of average 7.1×). Putting everything together, while a naive
L168@P1: IOMMU causes an average 95% performance overhead, our
L169@P1: NeuMMU effectively closes this gap, incurring only an average
L170@P1: 0.06% performance loss (Section IV).
L171@P1: With our robust NeuMMU design in hand, we then demonstrate the usefulness of MMU’s address translation feature for
L172@P1: handling embedding layers. We show that an MMU-less NPU
L173@P1: suffers from (redundant) manual data copy operations between
L174@P1: CPU and NPUs, leading to an average 71% performance
L175@P1: loss when executing embedding layers. Our NeuMMU again
L176@P1: effectively closes this performance gap using direct NUMA
L177@P1: accesses across remote memory regions, achieving significant
L178@P1: performance improvements than an MMU-less NPU design
L179@P1: (Section V). To summarize our key contributions:
L180@P1: • To our knowledge, this work is the first to explore
L181@P1: architectural support for NPU MMUs, a significant first
L182@P1: step in exploring this emerging design space.
L183@P1: • We conduct a detailed, data-driven analysis on conventional (dense) DNNs and emerging (sparse) embedding
L184@P1: layers, root-causing the limitations of GPU-centric IOMMUs in handling the bursty address translations of NPUs.
L185@P1: • We propose our throughput-centric NeuMMU design
L186@P1: based on our novel pending request merging buffer,
L187@P1: a high throughput parallel page-table walker, and a
L188@P1: translation path register, only incurring an average 0.06%
L189@P1: performance loss.
L190@P1: • Using DNN-based recommendation system models as
L191@P1: driving examples, we showcase how efficiently sparse
L192@P1: embedding layers can be handled using fine-grained
L193@P1: NUMA or page-migrations, enabled by NeuMMU.

L204@P2: II. BACKGROUND & METHODOLOGY
L205@P2: A. Address Translation in SPM-centric NPUs

L209@P2: threads as possible for latency tolerance [24] (Figure 2). In
